gap.headline: Two first-year units already give you real programming fundamentals — your advantage is six semesters of runway, and the plan spends it deliberately.

capabilities.name: Programming fundamentals

evidence.quote: design and write basic programs using a high-level procedural programming language

capabilities.rationale: Your first programming unit covers exactly what employers mean by fundamentals, and you can point to it.

capabilities.name: C and systems-level programming

evidence.quote: introduces students to a system programming language that gives programmers this kind of control

capabilities.rationale: You have written real C, which is more low-level exposure than most graduates bring.

capabilities.name: Data structures and algorithms

evidence.quote: explores a range of standard data structures and algorithmic techniques

capabilities.rationale: One unit has introduced the standard structures; a second pass will make this solid.

capabilities.name: Reasoning about performance and correctness
capabilities.rationale: Nothing you have done yet asks you to argue an algorithm is correct or efficient — that comes in second year.

capabilities.name: Testing discipline
capabilities.rationale: Assignments so far have not asked you to design tests, and employers treat testing as non-negotiable.

capabilities.name: Debugging real programs

evidence.quote: Read, write, test and debug typical small-scale programs

capabilities.rationale: You debug your own small programs; production debugging in an unfamiliar codebase is a step further.

capabilities.name: Git and version control
capabilities.rationale: No unit teaches it, every team expects it, and it is the single cheapest gap on this list to close.

capabilities.name: JavaScript, HTML and CSS
capabilities.rationale: Software developer ads in Australia ask for the web stack more than any other technology, and your degree has not touched it yet.

capabilities.name: SQL and relational databases
capabilities.rationale: Almost every backend role assumes you can model and query data; nothing on your transcript covers it yet.

capabilities.name: A cloud platform (AWS or Azure)
capabilities.rationale: In-demand in the ads and absent from coursework — one deployed project is how students usually close this.

capabilities.name: Docker, containers and CI
capabilities.rationale: This is production practice, not course content; a small pipeline on your own project is enough to talk about it.

capabilities.name: Linux and the command line
capabilities.rationale: You will meet it properly the first time you deploy something.

capabilities.name: Working in a team codebase
capabilities.rationale: Group work is not the same as branching, code review and merging — the workflow every employer runs.

capabilities.name: Explaining technical decisions

evidence.quote: Read, write, test and debug typical small-scale programs

capabilities.rationale: Coursework makes you justify decisions in writing; doing it for a non-technical audience is the remaining step.

roadmap.headline: Six semesters is enough to close every core gap without ever rushing — foundations first, habits that compound.
roadmap.stageNote: This plan is built for a first-year: light load, breadth before depth, and events with students in the room. A final-year with the same gaps would get a one-semester triage list instead.

steps.title: Put every assignment from now on in Git, pushed to GitHub
steps.rationale: Version control is learned by habit, not by course — starting now means three years of history by graduation.

steps.title: Rebuild your favourite COMP10001 project as a small command-line tool anyone can run
steps.rationale: Extending a unit you just finished, while it is fresh, is the cheapest first project you will ever build.

steps.title: Learn enough HTML, CSS and JavaScript to build one page that fetches and displays data
steps.rationale: The web stack tops Australian software ads and nothing in your degree will teach it — one page is the honest start.

steps.title: Go to one student-friendly tech event this semester — CISSA industry night or a beginner meetup
steps.rationale: The habit of walking into rooms is easier to build when the rooms are full of other students.

steps.title: Take COMP20003 and keep a public repo of the data structures you implement
steps.rationale: The unit does the teaching; the public repo turns coursework into evidence an employer can open.

steps.title: Learn SQL by putting a real dataset into SQLite and answering ten questions of your own
steps.rationale: Databases will not appear until later in your degree, and every role you are considering assumes them.

steps.title: Build and deploy a web app with a database to a cloud free tier, end to end
steps.rationale: One deployed project closes three gaps at once and becomes the centrepiece of every application you send.

steps.title: Add tests and a CI pipeline to your deployed project, then containerise it
steps.rationale: This is the difference between 'I built a thing' and 'I run a thing' — the sentence internship interviews reward.

steps.title: Start attending MelbJS or a practitioner meetup in your target stack
steps.rationale: By now you are past student events — the people at practitioner meetups are the ones who refer interns.

steps.title: Apply to graduate programs with the deployed project first on the resume, transcript second
steps.rationale: You will be applying with three years of Git history, one production project and a network — the position this plan was pointed at all along.
